query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a severe thermo‐mechanical processing route—in particular, a hybrid rolling treatment (e.g., an initial cryo‐rolling step followed by a warm‐rolling step) that refines the dual-phase lamellar colonies—will simultaneously enhance yield strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility compared with the as‐cast lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies (L12 and B2 phases) that exhibit micrometer-scale lamellae and numerous, relatively weak internal phase boundaries which are susceptible to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Perform a hybrid rolling process where the alloy undergoes severe plastic deformation—starting with cryo-rolling to accumulate stored strain energy and subsequently warm-rolling (e.g., near 600 °C) to promote controlled recrystallization—resulting in an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that inherits and refines the original lamellar architecture.
generation.conditions: The processing is conducted under tightly controlled deformation strain per pass and total strain (with the cryo-rolling and warm-rolling steps imparting identical incremental strains, cumulatively reaching high overall reduction in thickness), followed by evaluation under room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing. The thermomechanical parameters (strain rate, temperature during warm-rolling) are set to ensure sufficient grain refinement without losing the lamellar composite nature.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with decreased interlamellar spacing, enhanced phase boundary integrity, and an increased density of heterogeneous grain regions that foster internal back-stress and distribute strain more uniformly.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine, heterogeneous structure produced by the hybrid rolling improves the strength by providing enhanced dislocation storage and impediment to motion while simultaneously arresting and deflecting microcrack propagation along phase boundaries. The refined interfaces and increased back-stress from heterogeneous regions delay local strain localization, thereby elevating both yield strength and ductility relative to the coarse-colony baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to the as-cast lamellar baseline, the processed alloy will show an increase in yield strength and an improvement in tensile elongation at room temperature, indicating a better overall strength–ductility synergy.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-cast eutectic HEA featuring micrometer-scale dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation, resulting in limited room-temperature tensile ductility despite moderate strength.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy system under processing conditions that allow for sufficient severe plastic deformation (via cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling) and controlled recrystallization. It assumes that no deleterious phases form during processing and that the inherent lamellar nature is maintained.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvements—enhanced yield strength and ductility—are anticipated based on analogous processing studies, the exact quantitative magnitude of these improvements depends on fine details of the processing parameters (strain, temperature, rolling rate) that require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set processed by conventional casting (baseline) and another subjected to the hybrid rolling process (cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling with identical strain increments). Perform standardized room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Fractography to assess microcrack initiation and propagation at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid rolling processed samples do not exhibit simultaneous improvements in both yield strength and tensile ductility (i.e., if either property is not significantly higher than that of the as-cast baseline or if microcrack propagation is similar), then the hypothesis that the hybrid processing intervention improves the strength–ductility balance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractPhase-specific damage tolerance was investigated for the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high entropy alloy with a lamellar microstructure of L12 and B2 phases. A microcantilever bending technique was utilized with notches milled in each of the two phases as well as at the phase boundary. The L12 phase exhibited superior bending strength, strain hardening, and plastic deformation, while the B2 phase showed limited damage tolerance during bending due to micro-crack formation. The dimensionalized stiffness (DS) of the L12 phase cantilevers were relatively constant, indicating strain hardening followed by increase in stiffness at the later stages and, therefore, indicating plastic failure. In contrast, the B2 phase cantilevers showed a continuous drop in stiffness, indicating crack propagation. Distinct differences in micro-scale deformation mechanisms were reflected in post-compression fractography, with L12-phase cantilevers showing typical characteristics of ductile failure, including the activation of multiple slip planes, shear lips at the notch edge, and tearing inside the notch versus quasi-cleavage fracture with cleavage facets and a river pattern on the fracture surface for the B2-phas

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Unlike microstructural heterogeneities, which have been investigated so far to achieve strength-ductility synergy in different materials,, including HEAs,,, the novel strategy developed in the present research leads to a different paradigm featured by dual structural-compositional heterogeneities. On the microstructural side, the heterogeneities are ensured by the presence of the LRs and NCRs, while on the compositional side it is featured by a number of different constituents. While the LRs consist of L12 and B2 (containing disordered nano-precipitates), the NCRs contain different ordered and disordered phases with differences in structure, composition and internal strain or defect densities. Evidently, the dual structural-compositional heterogeneities offer a large number of interfaces and boundaries separating widely different hardness domains and phases. The massive back-stress strengthening in such heterogeneous microstructural arrangements results in super-strong EHEA coupled with appreciable ductility.
